stated.value: Water content in a petroleum line
In another building, remote from the process
Existing silica fiber cable from a visible or NIR setup, to be reused
MIR ATR measurement with the analyzer remote and the silica fiber reused

missing: Link length and fiber route (indoor/outdoor, bends, pulling/trenching)
Operating pressure, temperature and flow of the petroleum line

Expected water range (ppm, ppm-wt, % or free water) and required accuracy/detection limit
Hydrocarbon type (crude, refined product, lubricant), presence of H2S, emulsifiers, solids or particulates

status_reason: The enquiry can be assessed, but the concept as stated cannot be approved: silica fiber transmits only to roughly 2.2 to 2.5 um, while the MIR ATR water bands (about 2.9-3.0 um O-H stretch and 6.1-6.3 um H-O-H bend) lie beyond that limit. The water-in-petroleum problem itself is supported, with alternatives.
answer: The concept of reusing the silica fiber for MIR ATR cannot be approved, because silica fiber is opaque in the mid-infrared and would pass essentially no usable MIR signal over any practical link length. A feasible route is to test in-line NIR water detection (around 1.94 um, with the 1.45 um band as a check) through the existing silica fiber, and to use MIR ATR only in a laboratory or at a short, dedicated IR-transmitting path if MIR specificity is truly required. Link length, process conditions and hazardous-area data are needed before any final decision.

inline.headline: Do not reuse the silica fiber for MIR ATR; test in-line NIR water detection on it first
inline.method: NIR absorption spectroscopy of the water combination/overtone band near 1.94 um (with 1.45 um as a reference or check band), using a reflectance or transmission probe, with a short MIR ATR lab reference if needed
inline.probe: Robust NIR transmission or flow-cell probe with sapphire or quartz window, rated for line pressure and temperature, hazardous-area certified if required; alternatively a fiber-coupled ATR-NIR probe if a reflectance geometry is preferred
inline.install: Probe at a sample point with a flow-through or bypass cell to keep the window clean and the flow representative; if the analyzer must be remote, keep the fiber run short, shielded from heat and mechanical stress, and terminated in a protected junction box at the analyzer end
inline.fiber: Existing silica fiber is acceptable for NIR up to roughly 2 um over short-to-moderate lengths, but its attenuation, bend losses and length must be confirmed; it cannot be used for MIR. A chalcogenide, fluoride or hollow-waveguide IR fiber would be needed for any in-line MIR option, and those are limited in length and robustness
inline.test_against: Karl Fischer titration (coulometric for low ppm, volumetric for higher levels) on grab samples across the expected concentration range, plus lab FTIR/ATR as a MIR reference if MIR specificity is needed
inline.not_final_because: The link length, route, process conditions, hazardous-area class, water range and fiber specification are not supplied, and the NIR water signal in a petroleum matrix (with hydrocarbon overlap and possible emulsions or free water) has not been demonstrated

problems.text: Silica fiber absorbs strongly above about 2.2-2.5 um and cannot transmit the MIR ATR water bands near 3 um and 6 um, so the proposed MIR ATR measurement through this fiber will not produce a usable signal.

The MIR ATR crystal/probe must contact the process, but the analyzer is in another building; a remote MIR ATR cannot work with silica fiber, and an IR-transmitting fiber over a long route is not practical for a petroleum line.

The assumption that the existing visible/NIR fiber can be reused for a different spectral range is incorrect; a fiber must be selected for the wavelength band of the measurement, not reused across bands.
Water in petroleum is often at low ppm levels and may be dissolved, emulsified or free; a single absorption measurement may not represent it, and water-in-oil calibration is matrix-specific.
Hazardous-area classification of the tap point and the fiber route; any probe, junction box or electronics near the line must be certified for the zone.
Link length, bend radius, temperature exposure and mechanical protection of the existing fiber cable; NIR transmission over long lengths may be insufficient for weak water bands.
Process pressure, temperature and flow; the probe window and seals must be rated for these conditions, and fouling or wax/asphaltene deposition may affect the window.

methods.method: NIR absorption (water band near 1.94 um, check band 1.45 um) with silica fiber
methods.why: Silica fiber transmits in this range, water has strong NIR bands, and the existing fiber and possibly the existing spectrometer can be reused for a low-cost feasibility test.
Provides a MIR reference spectrum and specificity check for the water band, without requiring any MIR fiber in the process.
Primary reference method for water content in petroleum products; required for calibration and validation of any spectroscopic method.

methods.method: In-line MIR ATR with IR-transmitting fiber (chalcogenide, fluoride or hollow waveguide)
methods.why: Only relevant if NIR cannot resolve water in the matrix; would require a new MIR fiber, a short path to the analyzer and a certified probe, and is not compatible with the existing silica cable.

methods.method: MIR ATR through the existing silica fiber
methods.why: Silica is opaque in the mid-infrared, so the proposed concept cannot provide the MIR water signal.

questions.q: What is the total fiber link length, and what is the route (indoor, outdoor, underground, bends, number of connectors)?
questions.why: Determines NIR transmission loss and whether the silica fiber can support a usable signal.

questions.q: What are the line pressure, temperature, flow rate and composition (crude, refined product, lubricant)?
questions.why: Determines probe material, window and seal selection, and matrix interferences.

questions.q: What is the expected water concentration range and the required accuracy or detection limit (ppm, ppm-wt, % or free water)?
questions.why: Determines whether NIR sensitivity is adequate and which reference method is needed.

questions.q: What is the hazardous-area classification at the tap point and along the fiber route?
questions.why: Determines whether the probe, junction box and analyzer must be explosion-proof, purged or intrinsically safe.

questions.q: Can the measurement run on a bypass or sample loop, or must it be fully in-line?
questions.why: A bypass allows easier probe servicing and sample conditioning, and may move the analyzer closer to the process.

questions.q: What are the specifications of the existing silica fiber (core size, NA, length, connectors) and the visible/NIR spectrometer?
questions.why: Confirms whether the existing hardware can be reused for NIR water detection.

questions.q: Is water present as dissolved, emulsified or free water, and are H2S, solids, asphaltenes or waxes present?
questions.why: These affect the spectrum, the sampling approach and the probe fouling risk.

questions.q: Is a reference method (Karl Fischer or lab FTIR) available or acceptable for calibration?
questions.why: Calibration and validation of any spectroscopic method require reference data.

experiment.objective: Determine whether in-line NIR absorption through the existing silica fiber can measure water content in the petroleum line with adequate sensitivity and accuracy, and document that MIR ATR through silica is not viable.
steps: Collect the missing data: link length and route, process conditions, hazardous-area class, water range and fiber specification.
Record NIR transmission spectra (approximately 1.3-2.2 um) of the existing silica fiber over the actual or a representative length, with bends as installed, to quantify loss at 1.45 and 1.94 um.

Prepare a laboratory set of petroleum samples spanning the expected water range (for example by spiking dry oil with known water or using a water-saturated series), verified by Karl Fischer titration.

Measure the samples with the NIR setup (silica fiber, flow-through or transmission cell) and build a PLS or similar calibration on the 1.94 um band, with 1.45 um as a check, checking for hydrocarbon overlap.
Measure the same samples with lab FTIR/ATR to confirm the water band assignment and to show the MIR result for comparison.
Run a field trial at the tap point with a bypass or flow cell for at least one week, comparing in-line NIR results against periodic Karl Fischer samples across the process range.
Evaluate precision, detection limit, drift, window fouling, and response to temperature and flow variations; then decide on a final probe, install and hazardous-area design.
references: Karl Fischer titration (ASTM D6304 for coulometric water in petroleum products; ASTM D1744 for volumetric water in lubricating and petroleum-related liquids)
ASTM E1655 (practices for infrared multivariate quantitative analysis)
Published NIR water-in-oil studies using the 1.94 um O-H combination band
experiment.go_no_go: Go: NIR silica-fiber link transmits enough signal to resolve water at the required level with a calibration error within the customer's tolerance across the process range, and the probe meets hazardous-area and pressure requirements. No-go: insufficient signal over the link length, the water band is masked by matrix interference, or the probe cannot be installed safely at the tap point. MIR ATR through silica is a no-go regardless of results.

multispectral.combination: NIR (silica fiber, water band 1.94 um with 1.45 um check) for in-line monitoring, combined with lab FTIR/ATR (MIR) and Karl Fischer for calibration and reference only
multispectral.why: NIR fits the existing silica fiber and gives a practical in-line signal; MIR provides a specific reference for water and for interpreting the matrix, but cannot be carried by the silica fiber, so it stays in the laboratory unless a separate IR fiber is justified later.

assumptions: The silica fiber is a standard silica core/cladding fiber, not a fluoride, chalcogenide or hollow-waveguide IR fiber.
The existing visible/NIR setup can be adapted to measure the 1.3-2.2 um range, or a new NIR spectrometer will be used.
The petroleum line is a liquid process stream at a point where a flow cell or probe can be installed, and water is present in dissolved or emulsified form.
The link length is moderate (tens of meters); longer links may be impractical for NIR without signal amplification or a different fiber.
Hazardous-area requirements apply to the tap point and to the probe, and certified equipment will be selected accordingly.
No reference data or calibration models for water in this specific petroleum matrix exist yet.
